subject: Mathematics
status: DRAFT — for review by a Mathematics teacher before it is relied on
source: Drafted against the NCERT Class X Mathematics textbook (2025-26 rationalised reprint) and the 820 questions imported from C:/dev/sirah_project/NCERT/data. Topics follow the textbook's sections that remain in the rationalised syllabus; content CBSE removed in 2023 (Euclid's division lemma, cross-multiplication, completing the square, area of a triangle by coordinates, frustum, ogives) is deliberately absent.
notes: Chapter 6 is skipped: it is the seeded worked example and already carries authored outcomes (SIM-1 to SIM-5) and two concepts. SIM-4 (ratio of areas of similar triangles) was removed from the rationalised syllabus; that is for a teacher to decide, not this draft.

The imported bank still contains questions on removed content — Chapter 11 has items explicitly labelled '[Out of syllabus ...]', and Chapter 8 has complementary-angle items. No outcome here covers them, on purpose: linking them would make removed content count towards a student's mastery.

outcomes.statement: Writes a composite number as a product of its prime factors, and states that this factorisation is unique apart from the order of the factors.
Calculates the HCF and LCM of two or three numbers from their prime factorisations.
Uses the relation HCF × LCM = product of two numbers to find an unknown HCF, LCM or number.
Solves word problems about events that recur together, or the largest equal division, by recognising them as LCM or HCF problems.
Proves that numbers such as √2, √3 and √5 are irrational, using proof by contradiction and the uniqueness of prime factorisation.
Classifies sums and products of rational and irrational numbers as rational or irrational, and justifies the classification.

concepts.name: Irrational numbers and proof by contradiction

topics.title: Geometrical meaning of the zeroes of a polynomial

outcomes.statement: Identifies the degree of a polynomial and whether it is linear, quadratic or cubic.
Interprets the zeroes of a polynomial as the x-coordinates where its graph meets the x-axis, and reads the number of zeroes from a graph.
Uses factorisation to find the zeroes of a quadratic polynomial and verifies the relationship between the zeroes and the coefficients.
Calculates the sum and product of the zeroes of a quadratic or cubic polynomial directly from its coefficients.
Evaluates symmetric expressions in the zeroes, such as α² + β² or 1/α + 1/β, without finding the zeroes themselves.
Constructs a quadratic polynomial when the sum and product of its zeroes are given, and finds an unknown coefficient from a known zero.
Uses the ratios of coefficients to decide whether a pair of linear equations has a unique solution, no solution or infinitely many solutions.
Relates intersecting, parallel and coincident lines to consistent, inconsistent and dependent pairs of equations.
Calculates the value of an unknown constant for which a pair of linear equations has no solution or infinitely many solutions.
Solves a pair of linear equations in two variables by the substitution method.
Solves a pair of linear equations in two variables by the elimination method.
Writes a pair of linear equations from a word problem about costs, ages, numbers or speeds, solves it and interprets the answer.

concepts.name: Consistency of a pair of linear equations
Solving a pair of linear equations

outcomes.statement: Identifies whether a given equation is quadratic by reducing it to the standard form ax² + bx + c = 0.
Solves a quadratic equation by splitting the middle term and factorising.
Solves a quadratic equation using the quadratic formula.
Writes a quadratic equation for a situation involving areas, ages, numbers or speeds, solves it, and rejects a root that makes no sense in context.
Calculates the discriminant b² − 4ac and uses it to state whether the roots are real and distinct, real and equal, or not real.
Calculates the value of an unknown constant for which a quadratic equation has equal roots.
Uses the sum and product of the roots of a quadratic equation to find the other root or an unknown coefficient.

concepts.name: Nature of the roots of a quadratic

outcomes.statement: Identifies whether a list of numbers is an arithmetic progression and finds its first term and common difference.
Applies aₙ = a + (n − 1)d to find a given term, the position of a term, or the number of terms in an AP.
Solves for the first term and common difference when two terms of an AP are known, including terms counted from the end.
Uses the condition 2b = a + c to find an unknown for which three quantities are consecutive terms of an AP.

topics.title: Sum of the first n terms of an AP

outcomes.statement: Calculates the sum of the first n terms of an AP using Sₙ = n/2[2a + (n − 1)d] or Sₙ = n/2(a + l).
Calculates how many terms must be taken for a given sum, or recovers a term from an expression for Sₙ.
Solves word problems about savings, instalments, rows of objects or sums of multiples by modelling them as an AP.

concepts.name: nth term of an arithmetic progression

outcomes.statement: Calculates the distance between two points, and the distance of a point from the origin or from an axis.
Uses the distance formula to decide whether three points are collinear or form a particular triangle or quadrilateral.
Calculates the coordinates of the mid-point of a line segment.
Applies the section formula to find the point dividing a segment internally in a given ratio, and finds the ratio in which a point divides a segment.
Solves for an unknown coordinate when a mid-point or a point of division is known.
Defines the six trigonometric ratios of an acute angle in a right triangle, and writes each as a ratio of named sides.
Calculates the remaining trigonometric ratios when one ratio of an acute angle is given, using Pythagoras' theorem.
States the values of the trigonometric ratios of 0°, 30°, 45°, 60° and 90°.
Evaluates expressions built from the ratios of specific angles, and finds an angle from the value of a ratio.
States the identities sin²A + cos²A = 1, 1 + tan²A = sec²A and 1 + cot²A = cosec²A.
Proves a trigonometric identity, or simplifies an expression, using the fundamental identities.

concepts.name: Trigonometric ratios of an acute angle

outcomes.statement: Identifies the line of sight, the angle of elevation and the angle of depression in a described situation.
Draws the right triangle for a heights-and-distances situation and marks the known angle and side.
Calculates a height or a distance using one angle of elevation or depression.
Solves problems that combine two angles of elevation or depression, such as two ships seen from a cliff or a flagstaff on a building.
Distinguishes a tangent from a secant, and states how many tangents can be drawn from a point inside, on or outside a circle.
Uses the theorem that a tangent is perpendicular to the radius through the point of contact to find a length or an angle.

topics.title: Number of tangents from a point on a circle

outcomes.statement: Applies the theorem that the lengths of the two tangents from an external point are equal to find an unknown length.
Calculates angles formed by two tangents from an external point, the radii to the points of contact and the centre.
Proves results about a quadrilateral whose sides touch a circle, such as AB + CD = AD + BC.

topics.title: Areas of sector and segment of a circle

outcomes.statement: Calculates the length of an arc of a sector from its radius and central angle.
Calculates the area and the perimeter of a sector, including a quadrant, from its radius and central angle.
Calculates the central angle or the radius of a sector when its area or arc length is given.
Calculates the area of a minor or major segment by subtracting the area of the triangle from the area of the sector.
Solves applied problems such as the area swept by a clock hand or a wiper by modelling them as a sector.

concepts.name: Arc length and area of a sector
Area of a segment of a circle

topics.title: Surface area of a combination of solids

outcomes.statement: Identifies the basic solids that make up an everyday object, such as a cone on a hemisphere or a cylinder with a conical top.
Calculates the total surface area of a combined solid by adding only the surfaces that remain exposed.

topics.title: Volume of a combination of solids

outcomes.statement: Calculates the volume of a combined solid by adding or subtracting the volumes of its parts.
Solves problems about capacity and material, such as the air in a tent or the wood left after a cavity is hollowed out.
Calculates the mean of grouped data by the direct method using class marks.
Calculates the mean of grouped data by the assumed-mean and step-deviation methods, and explains why each gives the same answer.
Calculates a missing frequency when the mean of a distribution is given.

topics.title: Mode and median of grouped data

outcomes.statement: Identifies the modal class and calculates the mode of grouped data using the mode formula.
Identifies the median class from cumulative frequencies and calculates the median of grouped data.
Uses the empirical relationship 3 Median = Mode + 2 Mean to find one measure from the other two.

concepts.name: Median and mode of grouped data

outcomes.statement: States that the probability of an event lies between 0 and 1, and identifies impossible and sure events.
Applies P(not E) = 1 − P(E) to find the probability of the complement of an event.
Calculates the probability of an event with equally likely outcomes, such as drawing a card, a ball or a numbered ticket.
Lists the outcomes of an experiment with two dice or two coins and calculates the probability of a compound event from that list.
Uses a given probability to find an unknown number of items, such as the number of defective bulbs in a lot.

concepts.name: Probability with two dice or coins

prerequisites.requires: Plotting points on the coordinate plane
prerequisites.why: The graphical method is plotting, so placing and reading points has to be automatic before the method is worth anything.
A quadratic equation is a quadratic polynomial set equal to zero, so its roots are that polynomial's zeroes under another name.

prerequisites.why: Sin, cos and tan only exist because similar right triangles have identical side ratios.

prerequisites.why: Every surface-area formula here is a flat area wrapped around a solid, so the flat areas have to be solid first.
